title: Mock how somebody actually animates an icon
goal: There is no picture anywhere of what animating an icon in this app looks like, so nobody can say whether it should feel like editing a video or like something else entirely. Draw the flows as clickthroughs, the same way the video flows are drawn, so there is something real to look at and argue with before any of it is built.
notes:
First of three, and the only one that produces new pictures. The next task compares these with the video flows; the one after decides whether the app needs project types. Neither can start until there is something to compare.

Pick the scenarios from what somebody would really do, not from a feature list. An icon that pulses, a spinner that loops forever, a toggle that animates between two states, and a mark that draws itself on are the four that cover most of what people make animated SVGs for, and they stress different things: repetition, easing, two named states, and animating a path rather than a transform.

Resist designing the timeline in these pages. Draw what the person does and what they see; if a timeline turns out to be the answer, the comparison task will say so, and if something simpler works for icons then drawing a video timeline here will have talked everybody into the wrong thing.

---
SHARED CONTEXT for the animation and video alignment study (asked for by the user on 2026-09-14).

The user's words: "We also don't have usage clickthroughs for creating animated svgs so its unclear if anything could align with the clickthroughs of editing videos. We might want to figure out if there are opportunities to consolidate experience flows at all before building by mocking some flows up first and seeing how it will work. I want it to make sense for the user's usage scenario, and we might need different project types to isolate/hide some of the scenarios."

THIS IS A STUDY, NOT A BUILD. Nothing in this set changes Sources/. The deliverable is mocks and a written recommendation the user decides on. Do not start building a timeline, a keyframe model or a project type off the back of it; the whole point is to find out what to build before building it.

WHAT EXISTS, checked rather than assumed:
- Ten video clickthroughs under docs/design/mocks/pages: video-entry-wt, video-cut-wt, video-move-wt, video-zoom-wt, video-transition-wt, video-freeze-wt, video-title-wt, video-captions, video-compositing, video-speed.
- Six drawing ones: vector-wt, icon-draw-wt, icon-gradient-wt, draw, draw-boolean, iconography.
- ZERO for animating anything. The user is right: there is nothing to compare against.
- No project type concept in the app at all. A document is a canvas with a size (AppCoordinator.newBlankCanvasWindow(size:), File > New Blank Canvas). There is no kind, no template, nothing that hides one scenario's tools from another.
- Video today is a SEPARATE editor from the layer document: VideoEditorState and VideoEditorView, single clip, trim and crop and export. TrimTimeline and PlaybackScrubber are SwiftUI views bound to VideoEditorState, not a reusable time model, and PhotonzCore has no notion of time or keyframes at all. So the "shared foundation" is not something being reused; it is something that would have to be built, which is exactly why the user wants to look before leaping.

THE QUESTION UNDERNEATH, worth holding on to while mocking: the two things genuinely overlap in ONE place, a document that has a duration, a playhead and keyframes on properties. They diverge everywhere else. Video is sampled media: codecs, audio, frame scheduling, large data. Animated SVG is declarative: properties animate and the export emits SMIL or CSS and never rasterizes at all. A mock that pretends those are the same surface will look tidy and mislead everybody.

Conform to the shared mock library rather than inventing: docs/design/mocks/shared/UX-PATTERNS.md is the rulebook, docs/design/mocks/shared/AGENTS.md explains how pages are built, components/ holds the shared CSS and JS, and docs/design/mocks/dev-server.mjs serves them. A page that invents its own shell or its own controls cannot be compared with the video pages, which defeats the purpose.
acceptance: Clickthrough pages exist for the core animation scenarios, at minimum: giving a drawn icon a simple motion, editing the timing of that motion, previewing it looping, and getting it out as a file
Each page shows a whole flow from entry to result, the way the video walkthrough pages do, not a single screen
They use the shared mock library and conform to UX-PATTERNS, so they sit beside the video pages and can be compared with them rather than being a different-looking thing
The pages show what the person is trying to achieve, not a tour of controls: an icon that needs to wiggle, a loading spinner, a state change on a button
Where a flow needs something the app has no answer for, the page says so plainly rather than drawing a control that would have to be invented
Every page is reachable from the mock index and passes the existing mock checks
Audit under queue/audits/ with each page captured, and anything rough filed as a follow-up

log.note:
ADVERSARIAL REVIEW, before drawing anything. Walked the four scenarios as a person who has never seen a mock, and the video timeline does not survive the walk.

1) A video timeline is the wrong DEFAULT for icons. Video has a timeline because the document has a fixed duration full of sampled media at absolute times. An icon animation is under a second, it usually loops forever, and it has two to four keys. A 0-18s ruler under a 24x24 artboard is absurd, and an infinite spinner has no end to draw on it at all. Drawing one here would have talked everybody into the wrong thing, exactly as the task warned.

2) What a person arrives with is a NAMED MOTION, not keyframes. 'Make it spin', 'make the check draw on', 'make it pulse for attention'. So the shortest version that delivers the value is a Motion section in Properties: pick a motion, set how long, set repeat, done. No timeline at all for the 80% case. Keys are the escape hatch underneath, and the pages show them appearing only when you go and change one.

3) THE PREVIEW IS THE REVIEW, and it is the size strip, not a playhead. icon-draw-wt already ends by showing the glyph at 16/24/32/48 on light and dark, because that is how you judge an icon. For animation that same strip should be PLAYING. You never scrub an icon: scrubbing is for finding a frame, and icon work has no frame worth finding. This is the biggest single divergence from the video pages and it is deliberate.

4) The toggle case has no time axis whatsoever. Two states and how long the crossing takes. Two artboards side by side, not a playhead. Forcing it onto a timeline would be a lie about what the person is doing.

5) CUT as decorative: a scrubber, a transport bar, a ruler in seconds, a track list, per-frame stepping, audio. None of them earn their place on a 24 unit artboard.

Pages to draw: icon-animate-wt (pulse: give it motion, tune timing, watch it loop), icon-loop-wt (spinner: forever, no end), icon-states-wt (toggle: two states, one crossing), icon-drawon-wt (a mark that draws itself, animating the path not a transform), icon-export-anim-wt (getting it out, and what each destination can actually carry). Each page carries a visible note of what the app has no answer for.

BUILT. Five clickthroughs under docs/design/mocks/pages, all registered in the Icons group of the mock index:

icon-animate-wt   Make an icon pulse (9 steps) - motion as a named property, timing, looping preview, and the keys underneath at percent of a cycle
icon-loop-wt      Build a spinner that never stops (8) - forever with no end, and the transform origin mistake everybody makes once
icon-states-wt    Animate a toggle between two states (7) - two artboards, one crossing, no time axis, and the trigger hole said out loud
icon-drawon-wt    Draw a checkmark on (7) - animating the path not a transform, and the first flow with an order in it
icon-export-anim-wt  Hand the animated icon over (6) - destination before format, and what survives the trip

Every page carries a visible amber block at the top saying the app has no answer for any of it yet, which covers the acceptance item about not drawing controls that would have to be invented.

POST-BUILD REVIEW, run on the real pages in Chrome rather than read:
- All 37 steps across the five pages render with a visible cue, zero console errors, and reset/next/back/pause exercised on each.
- Found and fixed while reviewing: the preview button showed a play triangle while the preview was running. It is now driven by the same class the motion is, so a step that starts the motion cannot leave the wrong glyph on it, and the label is updated in data-tip because tooltip.js consumes and removes title.
- Found and fixed: the On artboard on the states page never appeared, because the column was revealed but the board inside it kept its own wt-off.
- Found and fixed: the destination menu on the export page opened over the canvas instead of under its own control.
- Gates: check-reserved, check-selection, check-a11y-names, check-shortcuts, check-elevation, check-states, check-fieldwrap all pass, audit-keyboard green across all 95 pages, all 95 pages return 200. Two gates bit for real and both fixes were improvements rather than appeasement: a borrowed .dot class name, and four pages that lit a Layers row while the canvas drew no selection, now declared with data-sel-frame and shown only while you are choosing the layer.
- Light theme and 980pt width checked. The only thing crossing the section box at 980 is the cue's own pulse ring, 9px, still inside the viewport with no horizontal scroll.

Audit at queue/audits/2026-09-14-icon-animation-flows.json with five browser captures.

FOLLOW-UPS. Nothing broke, so nothing clears the bar as a bug, and nothing is filed as a new task.

Folded into say-where-animating-an-icon-and-editing-a-video (the next task in this set): the three structural findings about where the two genuinely overlap, and the one gap this study leaves, which is that no page shows a whole SET animating together. That gap is the strongest case for a timeline and the comparison task is the right place to settle it, so it is a widening of that task rather than a new one.

Left rough, in this log rather than as tasks, because they are judgments for the user to react to on the audit rather than defects:
- left rough: five pages and 37 steps is a lot to read before forming a view. Mitigated by the audit's try list naming what each page proves in one line.
- left rough: the one cycle strip on icon-animate-wt is the closest thing in the set to a timeline and it is a hedge. If the comparison decides icons want a track, that strip is the seed of it.
- left rough: the five named motions (Pulse, Wiggle, Bounce, Spin, Breathe) are invented rather than researched, and preset lists grow. Raised as the open question on the page itself.
- left rough: on icon-states-wt the full explanation of why a tap cannot be exported needs the Properties panel scrolled; only the short version, 'needs the host', sits beside the control. The dock normalises every Properties group to 264px and overriding that for one page would break the thing that normalisation exists to fix, so this stays.
- left rough: the screenshots in the audit are browser captures of mock pages, not app captures. This task changes nothing under Sources, so there is no app surface to photograph and no playtest that could take one. Said plainly in the audit's rough list.

Five usage clickthroughs for animating an icon, under docs/design/mocks/pages and reachable from the Icons group of the mock index: icon-animate-wt (Make an icon pulse), icon-loop-wt (Build a spinner that never stops), icon-states-wt (Animate a toggle between two states), icon-drawon-wt (Draw a checkmark on), icon-export-anim-wt (Hand the animated icon over). They use the shared mock library and sit beside the video pages, and they deliberately carry no playhead, ruler or track list, with the reasoning written on each page. Every page opens with a visible note that the app has no answer for any of it yet. Verified in Chrome rather than assumed: all 37 steps render with a live cue, zero console errors, reset/back/next/pause exercised, light theme and 980pt width checked, and all seven mock gates plus audit-keyboard green across all 95 pages, which still all return 200.
